**Overview.** These problems drill [Week 4](week04.qmd). Problems 1–8 follow the lecture in order: message passing on trees, max-product, loopy BP, ancestral sampling, simple Monte Carlo, importance sampling, and rejection sampling. Problems 9–18, under [Homework 2 practice](#sec-w4p-hw2), go deeper on two techniques: loopy BP on a pixel grid and TrueSkill log-joints. Try each stem before opening the worked solution. Every graph, potential table, image, game record, and sample here is invented for practice. Notation matches the week chapter.

## Problem 1: Scheduling messages on a tree {#prb-1}

An undirected graph has six nodes and the edges
$$1\text{-}2,\quad 2\text{-}3,\quad 2\text{-}4,\quad 4\text{-}5,\quad 4\text{-}6.$$

1. Check that the graph is a [tree](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tree_(graph_theory)) and list its leaves. Would it still be a tree if we added the edge $1\text{-}3$?
2. How many messages does [belief propagation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Belief_propagation) send in total?
3. Which messages can be computed before any other message exists?
4. Which incoming messages must node 4 hold before it can send $m_{4\to2}$? Which must node 2 hold before it can send $m_{2\to1}$?
5. With node 2 as the root, list the messages of the inward pass and of the outward pass.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" .practice-answer title="Worked solution"}
This uses the tree definition in [Week 4, Trees and elimination order](week04.qmd#sec-trees) and the two-pass schedule in [Belief propagation on trees](week04.qmd#sec-bp).

1. Every node is reachable from node 2 (1, 3, 4 directly; 5, 6 through 4), so the graph is connected. A connected graph on 6 nodes with no cycles has exactly 5 edges, and this one has 5, so it has no cycles and is a tree. The leaves, the nodes with exactly one neighbour, are 1, 3, 5, and 6. Adding $1\text{-}3$ closes the cycle $1\text{-}2\text{-}3\text{-}1$, so the graph would no longer be a tree.
2. One message in each direction along each edge: $2|\mathcal E|=2\cdot5=10$.
3. A node can send to $i$ once it has heard from every neighbour other than $i$. A leaf has no other neighbours, so the product in the message formula is empty and it can send right away: $m_{1\to2}$, $m_{3\to2}$, $m_{5\to4}$, $m_{6\to4}$. Nodes 2 and 4 each have at least two neighbours they have not yet heard from, so they must wait.
4. $N(4)\setminus\{2\}=\{5,6\}$, so node 4 needs $m_{5\to4}$ and $m_{6\to4}$. $N(2)\setminus\{1\}=\{3,4\}$, so node 2 needs $m_{3\to2}$ and $m_{4\to2}$. The second of these itself waited on nodes 5 and 6, which is how $m_{2\to1}$ ends up summarizing the whole subtree on node 2's side.
5. Inward: $m_{1\to2}$, $m_{3\to2}$, $m_{5\to4}$, $m_{6\to4}$, then $m_{4\to2}$. Outward: $m_{2\to1}$, $m_{2\to3}$, $m_{2\to4}$, then $m_{4\to5}$, $m_{4\to6}$. That is $5+5=10$ messages, matching part 2.

**Answer.** (1) A tree with leaves 1, 3, 5, 6; adding $1\text{-}3$ makes a cycle. (2) 10. (3) The four leaf messages. (4) Node 4 needs messages from 5 and 6; node 2 needs messages from 3 and 4. (5) As listed above.
:::

## Problem 2: Sum-product on a three-node star {#prb-2}

Three binary spins $x_1,x_2,x_3\in\{+1,-1\}$ form a star with centre $x_2$: the edges are $1\text{-}2$ and $2\text{-}3$. The potentials are

- $\psi_1(+1)=1$, $\psi_1(-1)=2$, and $\psi_2=\psi_3=1$;
- $\psi_{12}(x_1,x_2)=3$ if $x_1=x_2$ and $1$ otherwise;
- $\psi_{23}(x_2,x_3)=2$ if $x_2=x_3$ and $1$ otherwise.

We observe $\bar x_3=+1$.

1. Compute $m_{1\to2}(x_2)$ and $m_{3\to2}(x_2)$, then the belief $b(x_2)=p(x_2\mid\bar x_3)$.
2. Check part 1 by writing out the unnormalized joint $\tilde p(x_1,x_2,\bar x_3)$ for all four settings of $(x_1,x_2)$.
3. To get $b(x_1)$, which extra message is needed? Compute it and the belief.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" .practice-answer title="Worked solution"}
This uses the message and belief definitions in [Week 4, Messages and beliefs](week04.qmd#sec-messages), including the rule for an observed sender.

1. Node 1 is an unobserved leaf, so it sums over its own value:
$$m_{1\to2}(+1)=\psi_1(+1)\cdot3+\psi_1(-1)\cdot1=3+2=5,$$
$$m_{1\to2}(-1)=\psi_1(+1)\cdot1+\psi_1(-1)\cdot3=1+6=7.$$
Node 3 is observed, so its value is plugged in rather than summed: $m_{3\to2}(x_2)=\psi_3(+1)\,\psi_{23}(x_2,+1)$, which is $2$ at $x_2=+1$ and $1$ at $x_2=-1$. The belief multiplies both in with $\psi_2=1$:
$$\tilde b(x_2)=(5\cdot2,\ 7\cdot1)=(10,\ 7),\qquad b(x_2)=\big(\tfrac{10}{17},\ \tfrac{7}{17}\big)\approx(0.588,\ 0.412).$$
The observation $x_3=+1$ pulls $x_2$ toward $+1$, while node 1's preference for $-1$ pulls the other way through a stronger edge. The observation wins, narrowly.
2. $\tilde p(x_1,x_2,\bar x_3)=\psi_1(x_1)\,\psi_{12}(x_1,x_2)\,\psi_{23}(x_2,+1)$:

    | $(x_1,x_2)$ | $(+1,+1)$ | $(-1,+1)$ | $(+1,-1)$ | $(-1,-1)$ |
    |---|---|---|---|---|
    | $\tilde p$ | $1\cdot3\cdot2=6$ | $2\cdot1\cdot2=4$ | $1\cdot1\cdot1=1$ | $2\cdot3\cdot1=6$ |

    Summing over $x_1$ gives $10$ at $x_2=+1$ and $7$ at $x_2=-1$, the same as $\tilde b(x_2)$. The messages did this sum in pieces.
3. Node 1 has one neighbour, node 2, so it needs $m_{2\to1}$. Node 2 multiplies in what it heard from its *other* neighbour, node 3, and sums out $x_2$:
$$m_{2\to1}(+1)=3\cdot2+1\cdot1=7,\qquad m_{2\to1}(-1)=1\cdot2+3\cdot1=5.$$
Then $\tilde b(x_1)=(\psi_1(+1)\cdot7,\ \psi_1(-1)\cdot5)=(7,\ 10)$, so $b(x_1)\approx(0.412,\ 0.588)$. The table agrees: $6+1=7$ at $x_1=+1$ and $4+6=10$ at $x_1=-1$.

**Answer.** (1) $m_{1\to2}=(5,7)$, $m_{3\to2}=(2,1)$, $b(x_2)=(10/17,\ 7/17)$. (2) The table sums to the same $(10,7)$. (3) $m_{2\to1}=(7,5)$, $b(x_1)=(7/17,\ 10/17)$.
:::

## Problem 3: Max-product against the most likely state of each node {#prb-3}

Two spins $x_1,x_2\in\{+1,-1\}$ share one edge, with node potentials equal to 1 and edge potential

| | $x_2=+1$ | $x_2=-1$ |
|---|---|---|
| $x_1=+1$ | 4 | 1 |
| $x_1=-1$ | 3 | 3 |

1. Run sum-product: compute both messages, both beliefs, and the setting $(\tilde x_1,\tilde x_2)$ that picks the more likely state of each node separately. What is its probability?
2. Run max-product and read off $\hat x_i=\arg\max_{x_i}b(x_i)$. What is the probability of $(\hat x_1,\hat x_2)$?
3. Explain the difference in one or two sentences.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" .practice-answer title="Worked solution"}
This uses [Week 4, Max-product BP and MAP inference](week04.qmd#sec-maxproduct).

The normalizer is $Z=4+1+3+3=11$, so the joint probabilities are the table entries divided by 11.

1. Sum-product sums over the sender:
$$m_{2\to1}(+1)=4+1=5,\qquad m_{2\to1}(-1)=3+3=6,$$
$$m_{1\to2}(+1)=4+3=7,\qquad m_{1\to2}(-1)=1+3=4.$$
So $b(x_1)=(5/11,\ 6/11)$ and $b(x_2)=(7/11,\ 4/11)$. Node by node, $\tilde x_1=-1$ and $\tilde x_2=+1$. The pair $(-1,+1)$ has probability $3/11\approx0.273$.
2. Max-product takes the largest term instead:
$$m_{2\to1}(+1)=\max(4,1)=4,\qquad m_{2\to1}(-1)=\max(3,3)=3,$$
$$m_{1\to2}(+1)=\max(4,3)=4,\qquad m_{1\to2}(-1)=\max(1,3)=3.$$
Both beliefs favour $+1$, so $(\hat x_1,\hat x_2)=(+1,+1)$, with probability $4/11\approx0.364$. This is the largest entry in the table, so it is the [MAP](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maximum_a_posteriori_estimation) estimate.
3. A sum-product belief adds up every configuration with $x_1$ in a given state. $x_1=-1$ wins that total ($3+3$ against $4+1$) without containing the single best configuration. A max-product belief scores only the best configuration in each state, so reading those off node by node gives the best joint setting.

**Answer.** (1) $b(x_1)=(5/11,6/11)$, $b(x_2)=(7/11,4/11)$; the node-by-node choice is $(-1,+1)$, probability $3/11$. (2) Max-product gives $(+1,+1)$, probability $4/11$, the MAP estimate. (3) Summed totals and best single configurations can disagree.
:::

## Problem 4: True or false on loopy BP {#prb-4}

Say whether each statement is true or false, with a one-line reason.

1. On a tree, running the loopy BP updates until they stop changing gives the exact marginals.
2. On a graph with cycles, loopy BP always converges if we run enough iterations.
3. With plain updates (no momentum), rescaling each new message so that it sums to 1 does not change the normalized beliefs.
4. On a graph with cycles, loopy BP beliefs are often more peaked than the true marginals.
5. Setting $\alpha=1$ in the momentum update gives back the plain update.
6. If a node's message to $i$ also multiplied in the message $i$ had sent it, beliefs on a tree would still be exact.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" .practice-answer title="Worked solution"}
This uses [Week 4, Loopy belief propagation](week04.qmd#sec-loopy) and the exclusion rule in [Messages and beliefs](week04.qmd#sec-messages).

1. **True.** On a tree the message updates are the same as BP, and the lecture states loopy BP is exact on trees.
2. **False.** The lecture says it may not converge at all, and messages can oscillate.
3. **True.** Each update is a sum of products that is linear in every incoming message, so a constant factor on one message passes through as a constant factor on later messages and beliefs. Normalizing the belief removes it, as in the three-node chain example. With momentum, scale does matter: blending $(1-\alpha)\,m^{\text{old}}+\alpha\,[\text{update}]$ weights the two vectors by their sizes as well as by $\alpha$. That is one reason to normalize before blending.
4. **True.** Evidence that leaves a node along one edge of a cycle can return along another and be multiplied in again, like hearing your own rumour back.
5. **True.** $(1-1)\,m^{\text{old}}+1\cdot[\text{update}]=[\text{update}]$.
6. **False.** Take the chain $x_1\text{-}x_2$. Then $m_{2\to1}$ would include $m_{1\to2}$, which already carries $\psi_1$, so the belief at $x_1$ would contain $\psi_1$ twice. The exclusion $k\ne i$ is what stops a node's own information from being counted twice.

**Answer.** True, false, true, true, true, false.
:::

## Problem 5: Ancestral sampling by hand {#prb-5}

A DAG over binary variables $A,B,C,D\in\{0,1\}$ has edges $A\to B$, $A\to C$, $B\to D$, $C\to D$, with

- $p(A=1)=0.3$;
- $p(B=1\mid A=0)=0.2$, $p(B=1\mid A=1)=0.7$;
- $p(C=1\mid A=0)=0.6$, $p(C=1\mid A=1)=0.1$;
- $p(D=1\mid B,C)=0.1,\ 0.5,\ 0.5,\ 0.9$ for $(B,C)=(0,0),(0,1),(1,0),(1,1)$.

To sample a binary variable with $p(\text{variable}=1)=\theta$, draw $u$ uniform on $[0,1]$ and set the variable to 1 if $u<\theta$.

1. Which of these are valid [topological orders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Topological_sorting)? (a) $A,B,C,D$ (b) $A,C,B,D$ (c) $B,A,C,D$ (d) $A,D,B,C$.
2. Visit the nodes in order $A,B,C,D$ using the uniforms $0.25,\ 0.81,\ 0.05,\ 0.47$. What sample do you get, and what is its probability under the joint?
3. Can this procedure give a sample from $p(A\mid D=1)$ directly? Why or why not?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" .practice-answer title="Worked solution"}
This uses [Week 4, Ancestral sampling](week04.qmd#sec-ancestral).

1. (a) and (b) are valid: $A$ comes before both its children, and $D$ comes after both its parents. Swapping $B$ and $C$ is fine because neither is a parent of the other. (c) puts $B$ before its parent $A$, and (d) puts $D$ before its parents $B$ and $C$, so both are invalid.
2. Each step uses the conditional with the parents set to values already drawn.
    - $A$: $0.25<0.3$, so $A=1$.
    - $B$: $p(B=1\mid A=1)=0.7$ and $0.81\ge0.7$, so $B=0$.
    - $C$: $p(C=1\mid A=1)=0.1$ and $0.05<0.1$, so $C=1$.
    - $D$: $p(D=1\mid B=0,C=1)=0.5$ and $0.47<0.5$, so $D=1$.

    The sample is $(A,B,C,D)=(1,0,1,1)$. Its probability is the product of the factors used: $0.3\cdot0.3\cdot0.1\cdot0.5=0.0045$.
3. No. $D$ is drawn last, from its parents, so its value is an output of the procedure, not something we can fix in advance. Nothing in the procedure sets $D=1$ and then updates $A$. The lecture notes that ancestral sampling draws from the joint with nothing observed and does not directly give conditional samples.

**Answer.** (1) (a) and (b). (2) $(1,0,1,1)$, probability $0.0045$. (3) No: the observed variable is a child, drawn last.
:::

## Problem 6: How many samples? {#prb-6}

1. A test function has $\mathrm{var}[\phi(x)]=9$ under $p$. How many independent samples does simple [Monte Carlo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monte_Carlo_method) need for the standard deviation of $\hat\Phi$ to be at most $0.1$? At most $0.05$?
2. We want $\mathbb P(x\in A)$ to within a standard deviation of $0.01$, using the [indicator function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indicator_function) as the test function. Show that $\mathrm{var}[\mathbf 1_{\{x\in A\}}]\le\tfrac14$ and find an $R$ that is enough whatever the true probability is. How many would suffice if we knew the probability was about $0.1$?
3. A grid with 50 points per axis is used to approximate $Z$ instead. How many grid points are there for $D=3$ and for $D=10$?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" .practice-answer title="Worked solution"}
This uses the variance formula in [Week 4, Simple Monte Carlo](week04.qmd#sec-simplemc) and the grid example in [Why the normalizing constant is hard](week04.qmd#sec-hardz).

1. $\mathrm{var}[\hat\Phi]=\mathrm{var}[\phi]/R=9/R$. A standard deviation of $0.1$ means variance $0.01$, so $R\ge900$. Halving the standard deviation to $0.05$ means variance $0.0025$, so $R\ge3600$. Halving the error costs four times the samples.
2. The indicator is 1 with probability $p$ and 0 otherwise, so its variance is $p(1-p)$, a parabola with its maximum $\tfrac14$ at $p=\tfrac12$. We need $p(1-p)/R\le0.01^2$. Using the bound, $R\ge0.25/0.0001=2500$ is enough whatever $p$ is. If $p\approx0.1$, then $p(1-p)=0.09$ and $R\ge900$ suffices.
3. $50^3=125{,}000$ points for $D=3$ and $50^{10}\approx9.8\times10^{16}$ for $D=10$. The grid grows exponentially with $D$ (the [curse of dimensionality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Curse_of_dimensionality)). The sample counts in parts 1 and 2 do not mention $D$ at all. The catch is that they assume we can already draw samples from $p$.

**Answer.** (1) $900$ and $3600$. (2) $p(1-p)\le\tfrac14$; $R=2500$ always suffices, $R=900$ if $p\approx0.1$. (3) $125{,}000$ and about $9.8\times10^{16}$.
:::

## Problem 7: Importance sampling with an unnormalized target {#prb-7}

A target on $\{1,2,3,4\}$ is known only up to a constant: $\tilde p=(1,\ 2,\ 4,\ 1)$. The proposal is uniform, $\tilde q(x)=1$ for every $x$. Five draws from $q$ come out as
$$1,\quad 3,\quad 3,\quad 2,\quad 4.$$

1. Compute the [importance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Importance_sampling) weights $\tilde w_r$ and the normalized weights $w_r$.
2. Estimate $\mathbb E_p[x]$ and compare it with the exact value.
3. Estimate $Z_p/Z_q$ and compare it with the exact value.
4. Suppose instead $\tilde q=(1,\ 1,\ 0.05,\ 1)$. What weight would a draw of $x=3$ get, and why is that a problem?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" .practice-answer title="Worked solution"}
This uses [Week 4, Importance sampling](week04.qmd#sec-importance).

1. $\tilde w_r=\tilde p(x^{(r)})/\tilde q(x^{(r)})=\tilde p(x^{(r)})$ here, giving $1,4,4,2,1$. They sum to $12$, so $w_r=\tfrac1{12},\tfrac4{12},\tfrac4{12},\tfrac2{12},\tfrac1{12}$.
2. The self-normalized estimate is $\sum_r x^{(r)}w_r=(1\cdot1+3\cdot4+3\cdot4+2\cdot2+4\cdot1)/12=33/12=2.75$. Exactly, $Z_p=8$ and $\mathbb E_p[x]=(1\cdot1+2\cdot2+3\cdot4+4\cdot1)/8=21/8=2.625$. Five samples land fairly close.
3. The average weight estimates $Z_p/Z_q$: $12/5=2.4$. Exactly, $Z_p=8$ and $Z_q=4$, so the ratio is $2$. Neither normalizer was needed to form the estimate in part 2; the ratio cancels in the self-normalized form.
4. $\tilde w=4/0.05=80$, against at most $2$ for the other values. The proposal rarely visits $x=3$, which holds half of $p$'s mass, so a run either misses it (and underestimates $\mathbb E_p[x]$) or hits it once and lets that one sample dominate the sum. This is the poor-coverage failure the week chapter warns about.

**Answer.** (1) $\tilde w=(1,4,4,2,1)$, $w=(1,4,4,2,1)/12$. (2) $2.75$ against $2.625$. (3) $2.4$ against $2$. (4) Weight $80$: one rare draw dominates.
:::

## Problem 8: Rejection sampling, and what dimension does to it {#prb-8}

Take $\tilde p(x)=x(1-x)$ on $[0,1]$ and the uniform proposal $q(x)=1$ on $[0,1]$, so $\tilde q=q$ and $Z_q=1$.

1. Find $Z_p$ and the smallest valid $c$. What is the acceptance rate?
2. With that $c$, decide accept or reject for these $(x,u)$ pairs, where $u$ was drawn uniform on $[0,\ c\,\tilde q(x)]$: $(0.2,\ 0.10)$, $(0.9,\ 0.12)$, $(0.5,\ 0.24)$, $(0.05,\ 0.03)$, $(0.7,\ 0.22)$.
3. What happens to the acceptance rate with $c=0.5$? What goes wrong with $c=0.2$?
4. Now take $D$ independent copies: $\tilde p(\mathbf x)=\prod_{d=1}^Dx_d(1-x_d)$ on the unit cube, with a uniform proposal on the cube. Find the acceptance rate for $D=10$ and $D=100$, and the expected number of proposals per accepted sample.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" .practice-answer title="Worked solution"}
This uses [Week 4, Rejection sampling](week04.qmd#sec-rejection), including the acceptance-rate formula at the end of that section.

1. $Z_p=\int_0^1(x-x^2)\,dx=\tfrac12-\tfrac13=\tfrac16$. The envelope must satisfy $c\cdot1\ge x(1-x)$ everywhere. The maximum of $x(1-x)$ is $\tfrac14$ at $x=\tfrac12$, so the smallest valid $c$ is $\tfrac14$. The acceptance rate is $Z_p/(cZ_q)=\tfrac16/\tfrac14=\tfrac23$.
2. Accept when $u\le\tilde p(x)$:
    - $\tilde p(0.2)=0.16\ge0.10$: accept.
    - $\tilde p(0.9)=0.09<0.12$: reject.
    - $\tilde p(0.5)=0.25\ge0.24$: accept.
    - $\tilde p(0.05)=0.0475\ge0.03$: accept.
    - $\tilde p(0.7)=0.21<0.22$: reject.

    The accepted samples are $0.2$, $0.5$, $0.05$.
3. $c=0.5$ is still a valid envelope, but the rate becomes $\tfrac16/\tfrac12=\tfrac13$: half as many acceptances for the same work. $c=0.2$ is invalid because $0.2<\tilde p(x)$ near $x=\tfrac12$. There every $u$ is at most $0.2$, so every proposal is accepted, and the accepted samples follow $\min(\tilde p(x),\,0.2)$ rather than $\tilde p$. The peak is flattened and the samples are no longer from $p$.
4. The product's maximum is $(\tfrac14)^D$, so the smallest $c$ is $(\tfrac14)^D$, while $Z_p=(\tfrac16)^D$ and $Z_q=1$. The rate is $(\tfrac23)^D$.
    - $D=10$: $(\tfrac23)^{10}\approx0.0173$, about 58 proposals per accepted sample.
    - $D=100$: $(\tfrac23)^{100}\approx2.5\times10^{-18}$, about $4\times10^{17}$ proposals per accepted sample.

    Each dimension multiplies the rate by $\tfrac23$, so it decays exponentially with $D$. This is the lecture's reason for presenting rejection sampling as a one-dimensional tool.

**Answer.** (1) $Z_p=\tfrac16$, $c=\tfrac14$, rate $\tfrac23$. (2) Accept, reject, accept, accept, reject. (3) Rate $\tfrac13$; $c=0.2$ is not an envelope and gives samples from the wrong distribution. (4) $(\tfrac23)^D$: about $0.017$ at $D=10$, about $2.5\times10^{-18}$ at $D=100$.
:::

## Homework 2 practice {#sec-w4p-hw2}

These problems go deeper on two Week 4 techniques. Problems 9–13 drill loopy BP messages and beliefs on a binary pixel grid. Problems 14–18 drill writing and evaluating a TrueSkill log-joint and reading quantities off posterior samples.

### Problem 9: Who talks to whom on a 3×3 grid {#prb-9}

A $3\times3$ binary image is flattened into a vector of $n=9$ pixels in [row-major order](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Row-_and_column-major_order), so node $s$ sits in row $\lfloor s/3\rfloor$ and column $s \bmod 3$:

$$\begin{matrix}0&1&2\\3&4&5\\6&7&8\end{matrix}$$

Use the 4-neighbour rule: with $m=3$, node $s$ has right neighbour $s+1$ unless $(s+1)\bmod m=0$, left neighbour $s-1$ unless $s\bmod m=0$, lower neighbour $s+m$ if $s+m<n$, and upper neighbour $s-m$ if $s-m\ge0$.

1. List the neighbours of node 0 (a corner), node 1 (an edge), and node 4 (the centre).
2. Messages are stored in an array `messages` of shape `(2, 9, 9)`, where `messages[:, j, i]` is the message from node $j$ to node $i$, entry 0 is the value at $x_i=+1$ and entry 1 the value at $x_i=-1$. Which slice holds $m_{4\to1}$?
3. When node 4 computes its message to node 1, which slices does it multiply together? Is the edge $4\text{-}1$ horizontal or vertical?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" .practice-answer title="Worked solution"}
This uses the message definition in [Week 4, Messages and beliefs](week04.qmd#sec-messages) and the grid model of [the denoising example](week04.qmd#sec-denoise).

1. Node 0: column 0 has no left neighbour and row 0 has no upper one, leaving $\{1,3\}$. Node 1: right 2, left 0, lower 4, no upper, so $\{0,2,4\}$. Node 4: all four exist, $\{1,3,5,7\}$. Corners have 2 neighbours, edges 3, interior pixels 4.
2. The sender is the middle index and the receiver the last, so $m_{4\to1}$ is `messages[:, 4, 1]`: `messages[0, 4, 1]` is $m_{4\to1}(+1)$ and `messages[1, 4, 1]` is $m_{4\to1}(-1)$.
3. The product runs over $k\in N(4)\setminus\{1\}=\{3,5,7\}$, and each factor is a message *into* node 4: `messages[:, 3, 4]`, `messages[:, 5, 4]`, `messages[:, 7, 4]`. The message `messages[:, 1, 4]` is left out, because node 4 does not echo back what node 1 told it. Nodes 4 and 1 share column 1 and sit in adjacent rows, so the edge is vertical.

**Answer.** (1) $N(0)=\{1,3\}$, $N(1)=\{0,2,4\}$, $N(4)=\{1,3,5,7\}$. (2) `messages[:, 4, 1]`. (3) The incoming messages from 3, 5, and 7 (second index = sender, third = 4); the edge is vertical.
:::

### Problem 10: One message, by hand {#prb-10}

In a denoising MRF with node potentials $\psi_j(x_j)=e^{\beta y_jx_j}$ and edge potentials $\psi_{ij}(x_i,x_j)=e^{Jx_ix_j}$, take $\beta=0.7$ and an edge $j\text{-}i$ with coupling $J=0.4$. Pixel $j$ is observed black, $y_j=-1$. Its three *other* neighbours currently send it these messages, written $\big(m(+1),\ m(-1)\big)$:

$$(0.6,\ 0.4), \qquad (0.7,\ 0.3), \qquad (0.45,\ 0.55).$$

1. Compute the unnormalized message $m_{j\to i}(x_i)$ for $x_i=+1$ and $x_i=-1$.
2. Normalize it.
3. The old message was $(0.5,\ 0.5)$. Apply the momentum update with step size $\alpha=0.6$.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" .practice-answer title="Worked solution"}
This uses the update rule of [Week 4, Loopy belief propagation](week04.qmd#sec-loopy) with the potentials of [the denoising example](week04.qmd#sec-denoise).

**Step 1: product of incoming messages, one number per state of $x_j$.**
$$x_j=+1:\ 0.6\cdot0.7\cdot0.45=0.189, \qquad x_j=-1:\ 0.4\cdot0.3\cdot0.55=0.066.$$

**Step 2: node potential.** With $y_j=-1$, $\psi_j(+1)=e^{-0.7}$ and $\psi_j(-1)=e^{0.7}$. The observation pulls $x_j$ toward black.

**Step 3: sum over $x_j$ for each $x_i$.** The edge potential is $e^{0.4}$ when $x_i,x_j$ agree and $e^{-0.4}$ when they disagree, and it combines with $\psi_j$ in the exponent:
$$m_{j\to i}(+1)=e^{-0.7+0.4}(0.189)+e^{0.7-0.4}(0.066)$$
$$=0.7408(0.189)+1.3499(0.066)=0.1400+0.0891=0.2291,$$
$$m_{j\to i}(-1)=e^{-0.7-0.4}(0.189)+e^{0.7+0.4}(0.066)$$
$$=0.3329(0.189)+3.0042(0.066)=0.0629+0.1983=0.2612.$$

**Normalize.** The total is $0.4903$, giving $(0.4673,\ 0.5327)$.

**Momentum.** $m^{\text{new}}=(1-\alpha)\,m^{\text{old}}+\alpha\,[\text{update}]$:
$$0.4\,(0.5,\ 0.5)+0.6\,(0.4673,\ 0.5327)=(0.4804,\ 0.5196).$$

Notice the tug of war. Two of the three neighbours lean white, which shows up as the larger product at $x_j=+1$, but the black observation multiplies the $x_j=-1$ branch by $e^{0.7}/e^{-0.7}\approx4$. The message ends up leaning slightly black. In code, the same three steps are an elementwise product, a $2\times2$ table of edge-times-node potentials, and a sum over one axis, as in [Week 3 practice, Problem 13](week03-practice.qmd#prb-13).

**Answer.** Unnormalized $(0.2291,\ 0.2612)$; normalized $(0.4673,\ 0.5327)$; after momentum $(0.4804,\ 0.5196)$.
:::

### Problem 11: From messages to a pixel decision {#prb-11}

A pixel $i$ in the same model ($\beta=0.7$) is observed white, $y_i=+1$. After message passing, its four neighbours send

$$(0.3,\ 0.7), \qquad (0.4,\ 0.6), \qquad (0.35,\ 0.65), \qquad (0.6,\ 0.4).$$

1. Compute the unnormalized belief $\tilde b(x_i)$ and the normalized belief $b(x_i)$.
2. Using the rule $\hat x_i=\arg\max_{x_i}b(x_i)$, what colour is the denoised pixel?
3. Suppose the last message had been stored unnormalized as $(6,\ 4)$. Does anything in part 2 change?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" .practice-answer title="Worked solution"}
This uses the belief formula of [Week 4, Messages and beliefs](week04.qmd#sec-messages) and the decision rule at the end of [the denoising example](week04.qmd#sec-denoise).

1. The node potential is $\psi_i(+1)=e^{0.7}=2.0138$, $\psi_i(-1)=e^{-0.7}=0.4966$. Unlike a message, a belief multiplies in *every* neighbour's message, with no exclusion:
$$\prod_jm_{j\to i}(+1)=0.3\cdot0.4\cdot0.35\cdot0.6=0.0252,$$
$$\prod_jm_{j\to i}(-1)=0.7\cdot0.6\cdot0.65\cdot0.4=0.1092.$$
So $\tilde b=(2.0138\cdot0.0252,\ 0.4966\cdot0.1092)=(0.0507,\ 0.0542)$, and dividing by the total $0.1050$ gives $b=(0.483,\ 0.517)$.
2. $b(-1)>b(+1)$, so $\hat x_i=-1$: black. Three of four neighbours lean black strongly enough to outvote the white observation, which is how the model removes an isolated flipped pixel.
3. No. Multiplying one message by 10 multiplies both entries of $\tilde b$ by 10, and normalizing removes it. This is the scaling argument of the week chapter's three-node chain example.

**Answer.** $\tilde b\approx(0.0507,\ 0.0542)$, $b\approx(0.483,\ 0.517)$; the pixel is set to black; rescaling a message changes nothing.
:::

### Problem 12: What the step size does {#prb-12}

Loopy BP on a cycle can oscillate. Take a toy version: a single message $(p,\ 1-p)$ whose freshly computed update is always the flipped vector $(1-p,\ p)$. Start from $p=0.8$ and apply the momentum update
$$m^{\text{new}}=(1-\alpha)\,m^{\text{old}}+\alpha\,[\text{update}].$$

1. Trace $p$ for three iterations with $\alpha=1$, $\alpha=0.5$, and $\alpha=0.25$.
2. Write $p^{\text{new}}-\tfrac12$ in terms of $p^{\text{old}}-\tfrac12$ and explain the three behaviours.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" .practice-answer title="Worked solution"}
This uses the momentum trick in [Week 4, Loopy belief propagation](week04.qmd#sec-loopy).

1. The first entry updates as $p^{\text{new}}=(1-\alpha)p+\alpha(1-p)$.
    - $\alpha=1$ (plain replacement): $0.8\to0.2\to0.8\to0.2$. It never settles.
    - $\alpha=0.5$: $0.5\,(0.8)+0.5\,(0.2)=0.5$, then $0.5$ forever.
    - $\alpha=0.25$: $0.75p+0.25(1-p)=0.25+0.5p$, so $0.8\to0.65\to0.575\to0.5375$.
2. Subtracting $\tfrac12$ from both sides,
$$p^{\text{new}}-\tfrac12=(1-2\alpha)\big(p^{\text{old}}-\tfrac12\big).$$
The distance from the fixed point $\tfrac12$ is multiplied by $1-2\alpha$ each iteration. At $\alpha=1$ the factor is $-1$: same size, opposite sign, a permanent oscillation. At $\alpha=0.5$ it is $0$ and the oscillation dies in one step. At $\alpha=0.25$ it is $\tfrac12$, so the distance halves each time with no sign flips.

Real BP updates are not this simple map, so no single step size zeroes out oscillation in general. The general point survives: blending in the old message shrinks the jump each iteration, which damps oscillation. The price is that when the plain updates would have converged anyway, a small $\alpha$ makes each iteration move less.

**Answer.** $\alpha=1$: $0.2, 0.8, 0.2$. $\alpha=0.5$: $0.5, 0.5, 0.5$. $\alpha=0.25$: $0.65, 0.575, 0.5375$. The deviation from $\tfrac12$ scales by $1-2\alpha$ per step.
:::

### Problem 13: Observation strength against coupling {#prb-13}

1. A binary symmetric channel flips each pixel with probability $\epsilon$. Compute $\beta=\tfrac12\log\frac{1-\epsilon}{\epsilon}$ for $\epsilon=0.1$ and $\epsilon=0.25$.
2. An interior pixel $i$ is observed black ($y_i=-1$). To isolate the trade-off, suppose its four neighbours are known to be white, so each sends the message $m(x_i)=e^{Jx_i}$ (one shared coupling $J$ on all four edges). Find the ratio $b(+1)/b(-1)$, and the condition on $J$ under which the pixel's belief favours white.
3. Evaluate that threshold for both values of $\epsilon$ from part 1.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" .practice-answer title="Worked solution"}
This uses the observation model and the posterior of [Week 4, Tutorial example: image denoising](week04.qmd#sec-denoise).

1. $\epsilon=0.1$: $\beta=\tfrac12\log9=\log3\approx1.099$. $\epsilon=0.25$: $\beta=\tfrac12\log3\approx0.549$. Noisier observations deserve less trust, and $\beta$ shrinks accordingly.
2. The node potential gives $e^{-\beta}$ at $x_i=+1$ and $e^{\beta}$ at $x_i=-1$. Each neighbour message gives $e^{J}$ versus $e^{-J}$, four times over. So
$$\frac{b(+1)}{b(-1)}=\frac{e^{-\beta}\,e^{4J}}{e^{\beta}\,e^{-4J}}=e^{8J-2\beta}.$$
The belief favours white exactly when $8J>2\beta$, that is $J>\beta/4$.
3. $\epsilon=0.1$: $J>0.275$. $\epsilon=0.25$: $J>0.137$.

The inequality is a vote. The observation contributes $2\beta$ toward black, and each agreeing neighbour contributes $2J$ toward white. With noisier data a weaker coupling is enough to outvote the observation. The inequality has no way of knowing whether the black pixel is noise or a genuine one-pixel detail of the image: it treats both the same.

**Answer.** (1) $\beta\approx1.099$ and $0.549$. (2) $b(+1)/b(-1)=e^{8J-2\beta}$; white wins when $J>\beta/4$. (3) $J>0.275$ and $J>0.137$.
:::

### Problem 14: The log-prior of independent skills {#prb-14}

Three players have independent [normal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Normal_distribution) priors $z_i\sim\mathcal N(0,1)$. Two candidate skill settings are stored as the rows of a $2\times3$ array:

$$\begin{pmatrix}0&1&-2\\0.5&0.5&0.5\end{pmatrix}.$$

1. Compute the log-prior $\log p(z_1,z_2,z_3)$ for each row.
2. Why is the joint log-prior a sum, and along which axis of this array does that sum run? What shape is the result?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" .practice-answer title="Worked solution"}
This uses the prior in the TrueSkill definition of [Week 4, Latent variables and the TrueSkill model](week04.qmd#sec-trueskill).

The standard normal log-density is $\log\mathcal N(z;0,1)=-\tfrac12\log(2\pi)-\tfrac12z^2$, and $\tfrac12\log(2\pi)\approx0.9189$.

1. Row 1: $-3(0.9189)-\tfrac12(0+1+4)=-2.7568-2.5=-5.257$. Row 2: $-2.7568-\tfrac12(0.75)=-3.132$.
2. Independence makes the joint prior a product $\prod_ip(z_i)$, and the log of a product is a sum of logs. Each row is one setting of all players, so the sum runs across the players within a row (axis 1, the column axis), leaving one number per row: shape `(2,)`. Summing down the columns instead would add the same player's log-density across two different settings, which is not the log of any probability in the model.

Row 2 scores higher because all three skills sit near the prior mean of 0; row 1 pays for the player at $-2$.

**Answer.** $-5.257$ and $-3.132$. A sum because of independence, taken across players (axis 1), giving shape `(2,)`.
:::

### Problem 15: Logs of sums without overflow {#prb-15}

Double-precision floats overflow above about $1.8\times10^{308}$, so $e^{a}$ is stored as infinity once $a$ exceeds roughly 709 ([arithmetic overflow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arithmetic_overflow)).

1. Compute $\log\big(e^{1000}+e^{998}\big)$ by hand, without ever forming $e^{1000}$.
2. The function $\mathrm{logaddexp}(u,v)=\log(e^u+e^v)$ is computed with the same trick. Write $\log(1+e^{a})$ using it. What does the naive formula `log(1 + exp(a))` return at $a=800$, and what is the correct value to many digits?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" .practice-answer title="Worked solution"}
This supports evaluating the logistic function of [Week 4, Latent variables and the TrueSkill model](week04.qmd#sec-trueskill) in log space.

1. Factor out the largest exponential (the [LogSumExp](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/LogSumExp) trick):
$$\log\big(e^{1000}+e^{998}\big)=1000+\log\big(1+e^{-2}\big)=1000+0.1269=1000.1269.$$
The only exponential left to evaluate is $e^{-2}$, which is harmless.
2. Since $1=e^0$, $\log(1+e^{a})=\mathrm{logaddexp}(0,a)$. Naively, `exp(800)` overflows to infinity and the log of infinity is infinity. Factoring out $e^{a}$ instead gives $800+\log(1+e^{-800})$, and $e^{-800}$ is so small that the answer is $800$ to all printed digits. For very negative $a$ the same trick avoids the opposite problem, where $e^{a}$ underflows toward 0 and the log goes to $-\infty$.

**Answer.** (1) $\approx1000.1269$. (2) $\log(1+e^a)=\mathrm{logaddexp}(0,a)$; the naive formula returns infinity at $a=800$, the true value is $800$ (to double precision).
:::

### Problem 16: A two-player posterior up to a constant {#prb-16}

Two players $A$ and $B$ have independent priors $z_A,z_B\sim\mathcal N(0,1)$ and the course's TrueSkill likelihood $p(A\text{ beats }B\mid z_A,z_B)=\sigma(z_A-z_B)$. They play four games: $A$ wins three and $B$ wins one.

1. Write $\log p(z_A,z_B,\text{games})$.
2. Evaluate it, dropping the constant $-\log(2\pi)$, at $(z_A,z_B)=(0,0)$, $(0.5,-0.5)$, and $(1.5,0.5)$. Which is most probable under the posterior?
3. Why can we draw the posterior's contour lines from $\log p(z_A,z_B,\text{games})$ without ever computing $p(\text{games})$?
4. Change variables to $d=z_A-z_B$ and $s=z_A+z_B$. Show that the likelihood depends only on $d$, and that the prior factorizes into a function of $d$ times a function of $s$. What does that say about what the games can teach us?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" .practice-answer title="Worked solution"}
This uses the joint distribution in [Week 4, Latent variables and the TrueSkill model](week04.qmd#sec-trueskill) and the unnormalized-density setting of [Sampling from an unnormalized density](week04.qmd#sec-sampling).

1. Prior times one factor per game, with games independent given the skills:
$$\log p=-\log(2\pi)-\tfrac12\big(z_A^2+z_B^2\big)$$
$${}+3\log\sigma(z_A-z_B)+\log\sigma(z_B-z_A).$$
2. Using $\log\sigma(0)=-0.6931$, $\log\sigma(1)=-0.3133$, $\log\sigma(-1)=-1.3133$:
    - $(0,0)$: likelihood $4(-0.6931)=-2.7726$, prior $0$; total $-2.773$.
    - $(0.5,-0.5)$: $d=1$, likelihood $3(-0.3133)-1.3133=-2.2530$, prior $-0.25$; total $-2.503$.
    - $(1.5,0.5)$: $d=1$ again, so the same likelihood $-2.2530$, prior $-\tfrac12(2.25+0.25)=-1.25$; total $-3.503$.

    $(0.5,-0.5)$ is the most probable of the three.
3. $p(z_A,z_B\mid\text{games})=p(z_A,z_B,\text{games})/p(\text{games})$, and the denominator does not depend on $(z_A,z_B)$. Dividing by a constant, or subtracting a constant in log space, shifts every height by the same amount, so the [level sets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Level_set) are the same curves; only their labels change.
4. The likelihood is a function of $z_A-z_B=d$ alone. For the prior, $z_A=\tfrac{s+d}{2}$ and $z_B=\tfrac{s-d}{2}$, so
$$z_A^2+z_B^2=\tfrac14\big[(s+d)^2+(s-d)^2\big]=\tfrac12\big(s^2+d^2\big),$$
and the prior is proportional to $e^{-d^2/4}\,e^{-s^2/4}$. (The change of variables also brings a constant Jacobian factor, which does not affect the shape.) The posterior is therefore $\big[e^{-d^2/4}\times\text{likelihood}(d)\big]\times e^{-s^2/4}$: the games update our belief about the skill *difference*, while the belief about the *sum* stays exactly at the prior. Part 2 shows this: $(0.5,-0.5)$ and $(1.5,0.5)$ share $d=1$ and get the same likelihood, and only the prior separates them.

**Answer.** (2) $-2.773$, $-2.503$, $-3.503$; $(0.5,-0.5)$ is highest. (3) The normalizer is a constant shift. (4) Likelihood in $d$ only, prior $\propto e^{-d^2/4}e^{-s^2/4}$, so data inform $d$ and leave $s$ at its prior.
:::

### Problem 17: Looking up skills game by game {#prb-17}

Four players have skills `z = np.array([0.5, -1.0, 2.0, 0.0])`. Five games are stored one per row as (winner index, loser index):

```python
games = np.array([[2, 0],
                  [0, 1],
                  [3, 1],
                  [2, 3],
                  [1, 0]])
```

What does `z[games[:, 0]] - z[games[:, 1]]` evaluate to, and what does each entry mean in the model?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" .practice-answer title="Worked solution"}
This sets up the "one factor per game" product of [Week 4, Latent variables and the TrueSkill model](week04.qmd#sec-trueskill).

- `games[:, 0]` is the winner column `[2, 0, 3, 2, 1]`, and indexing `z` with an integer array returns one entry per index: `z[games[:, 0]]` is `[2.0, 0.5, 0.0, 2.0, -1.0]`.
- `games[:, 1]` is `[0, 1, 1, 3, 0]`, so `z[games[:, 1]]` is `[0.5, -1.0, -1.0, 0.0, 0.5]`.
- The elementwise difference has shape `(5,)`, one entry per game.

Each entry is $z_{\text{winner}}-z_{\text{loser}}$, the argument of $\sigma$ in that game's likelihood factor. Positive entries are games the stronger player won. The last entry, $-1.5$, is an upset: player 1 beat a player rated higher, so its factor $\sigma(-1.5)\approx0.18$ is small. Player indices may repeat across rows, which is how several games between the same pair, or one player in many games, are handled with no loop.

**Answer.** `array([ 1.5,  1.5,  1. ,  2. , -1.5])`: the winner-minus-loser skill gap for each game.
:::

### Problem 18: A probability from posterior samples {#prb-18}

Suppose some sampler has produced eight draws from a joint posterior over two players' skills $(z_i,z_j)$:

| $r$ | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 | 6 | 7 | 8 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| $z_i$ | 1.2 | 0.4 | 1.5 | 0.9 | 0.3 | 1.1 | 1.8 | 0.7 |
| $z_j$ | 0.8 | 0.9 | 1.1 | 0.2 | 0.6 | 1.3 | 0.7 | 0.4 |

1. Estimate $\mathbb P(z_i\ge z_j\mid\text{games})$.
2. Estimate the posterior mean and standard deviation of $z_i$.
3. If the draws were independent, roughly how uncertain is the estimate in part 1?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" .practice-answer title="Worked solution"}
This uses [Week 4, What sampling is for](week04.qmd#sec-goals) and [Simple Monte Carlo](week04.qmd#sec-simplemc).

1. A probability is the expectation of an indicator function: $\mathbb P(z_i\ge z_j)=\mathbb E\big[\mathbf 1_{\{z_i\ge z_j\}}\big]$. The simple Monte Carlo estimate is the fraction of samples where the event holds. Row by row the indicator is $1,0,1,1,0,0,1,1$, so the estimate is $5/8=0.625$.
2. Mean: $\hat\Phi_1=7.9/8=0.9875$. For the spread, use the second test function $\phi_2=z_i^2$: $\hat\Phi_2=9.69/8=1.2113$, so the variance estimate is $\hat\Phi_2-\hat\Phi_1^2=1.2113-0.9752=0.2361$ and the standard deviation is $0.486$.
3. The indicator has variance $p(1-p)$, so with independent draws $\mathrm{var}[\hat\Phi]=p(1-p)/R\approx0.625\cdot0.375/8=0.029$, a standard deviation of about $0.17$. Eight samples cannot pin the probability down. The $1/R$ rate assumes independent draws; samplers that produce each draw from the previous one (next week's topic) give correlated samples, and then the error shrinks more slowly than this formula says.

**Answer.** (1) $0.625$. (2) Mean $0.9875$, standard deviation $\approx0.486$. (3) About $\pm0.17$ (one standard deviation) for independent draws.
:::
